units: the writer is writing to a friend from a shared garden
the young plants were no longer coming up out of the seed
the surface of the ground had hardened into a tight crust
water slid off toward a drainage ditch instead of soaking down to the roots
a grower from a nearby plot suggested a tried remedy
the soil material was sifted to take out the stones
an organic amendment was mixed in to keep water available
the surface is broken up after every watering
the plants came up after about three weeks
text: Dear friend, I am writing from the shared garden I told you about back in the spring. For weeks nothing came up. The seed stayed shut and none of us could figure out what was holding it. Then we looked closer. The top of the bed had baked into a hard crust, and every drop we poured ran sideways into the drainage ditch instead of sinking down to the roots. A grower from the plot next door told us what he does. We put the soil through a sieve and picked out the stones, then worked in well rotted compost, which holds moisture without smothering anything small. Now we scratch the surface open after every watering. About three weeks later the first leaves broke through, thick and green. I will send you a picture of the row once it fills in. Write back and tell me whether your balcony has finally given you anything.

units: an insect specialist compares two kinds of pollinators
kept colonies hold a very large number of workers
kept foragers travel long distances
wild species nest on their own in hollow stems or sandy banks
wild species range over a small radius
wild species work flowers the others pass over
the specialist will not name one kind as better
an orchard leaning on hives alone gives an uneven crop
ground with few flowers defeats both kinds
text: So are wild bees worth as much as kept bees when it comes to pollination? The question comes up again and again, and an insect specialist I put it to answered me with a comparison. Hive bees go out in huge numbers, thousands of workers to a colony, and they will fly a long way for a crop. Their strength is sheer weight of bodies. Wild bees do the opposite. Each one nests alone in a hollow stem or a sandy bank, stays close to home, and works the flowers the others pass over. Their strength is precision. So which one do you pick? Neither, she said, laughing. An orchard leaning on hives alone brings in an uneven crop, since a share of the blossom opens on cold days, when the hive stays shut. Then she put a limit on all of it. On ground with no wild flowers left, she said, neither kind will hold out.

units: the head of a laboratory presents her monitoring beside a body of water
she lists the signs used to judge a stream
insect larvae living under the stones are the first sign
the loss of those larvae points to pollution
algae spreading over the bottom betrays fertilizer coming off farmland
a bright floating object serves to gauge the speed of the current
the state of the banks is among the signs people overlook
a bank without plants gives way at the first rise in water
bankside shrubs hold the soil and shelter birds
a proper reading calls for repeated visits
text: The head of the laboratory meets us at the edge of a shallow pond with a hand lens ready. She runs through the signs her team looks for when it judges whether a stream is healthy. Start with the insects clinging under the stones, she says. Their larvae cannot cope with fouled water, so a bare stone bed points to pollution. Next comes the algae coating the bottom. Once that coat thickens, fertilizer has leached in from the fields upslope. Third is the speed of the current, which a bright float will gauge well enough. Then she names a sign that hardly anyone bothers with, the bank itself. A bare edge slumps away with the first rise in the water, while a bank held by shrubs keeps its soil and shelters the birds that nest close to the surface. None of this, she finishes, shows up in a single visit.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: a glass worker notices the magnifying effect of a curved piece of glass
clear stones were shaped and rubbed smooth to read fine writing
wooden frames were made to hold the gap between the eye and the lens
those frames left the hands free
a lens maker set two glasses one above the other inside a tube
that stacking raised the magnification further
tiny living things were seen in standing water
living beings inside a single drop astonished the learned
color faults along the rim were corrected as the craft improved
the instrument ended up making the basic unit of life visible
text: Long before anyone thought to call it science, a glass worker noticed that a swollen chip of glass thickened the threads of the cloth beneath it. Curiosity did the rest. Clear stones were ground and rubbed smooth so that cramped writing could be read at last. Wooden frames followed, holding the glass a fixed distance from the eye and leaving both hands free. Then a lens maker set two glasses one above the other inside a tube, and the image swelled further still. A patient watcher turned such a tube on stale water and found tiny creatures twitching in it. That a whole living thing could fit inside one drop shook the learned men of the day. Later hands polished better and cleared away the colored fringes that blurred the rim, until the glass gave up the cell itself. What the naked eye withheld, the glass granted.

units: a dried seed puts its biological activity on hold
that state lets it survive extreme conditions
taking up water swells the tissues and splits the protective coat
the arrival of water wakes enzymes
those enzymes turn the stored starch into usable sugars
the root heads downward under gravity
the shoot grows in the opposite direction
mild warmth speeds the work of the enzymes
excessive heat wrecks the enzymes and halts emergence
waterlogged ground drives out the oxygen and rots the seedling
text: A dry seed does nothing at all. Its chemistry is on hold, and in that state it comes through cold and drought that would kill a growing plant outright. Let moisture through the coat and the tissues swell until the pressure splits the shell. The water also wakes a set of enzymes, and these break the stored starch down into sugars the embryo can burn. Growth follows. A root pushes down, pulled that way by gravity, while a shoot climbs the other way. Warmth speeds the whole business up, since enzymes work faster in a mild bed. Push the heat too high, though, and they fall apart, and the seedling never reaches the surface. Too much water does comparable harm. It drives the air out of the ground, starves the tissues of oxygen and rots the young stem before a leaf ever opens.

units: a seed conservation station rewrote its procedure after a technical fault
the smallest seeds clung to the metal surfaces of the sorting machine
that clinging built up into lumps
the weight readings came out wrong
the worker felt an electric shock near the feed hopper
seeds rubbing against dry metal were producing static electricity
replacing the equipment lay beyond what the site could pay
an engineer advised running a conductor from the metal parts down to the ground
she also advised keeping damp in the air of the room
the fault was gone by the following harvest
text: At a station where seed is kept and sorted, a small mishap ended in a whole procedure being rewritten. The worker running the sorter found that the finest seed was sticking to the metal walls of the machine and gathering there in lumps, so that not one of the weighings came out right. Reaching toward the feed hopper, he took a sharp shock, and a pale spark jumped across to the panel. Static, raised by dry husks rubbing on dry steel, accounted for the whole fault. Management thought first of replacing the line, an outlay far beyond what the station could carry. An engineer put forward two much plainer measures. Run a copper wire from every metal part down to the ground, she said, and hold a moderate damp in the air of the room with a fine mist. The lumps were gone by the following harvest, and the weights could be trusted once more.

units: the kit takes in a clear jar, a mesh sieve, a funnel, a pair of tweezers and a magnifying glass
two separate methods serve to pull the living things out of a soil sample
the two methods answer different aims
the dry method means shaking the crumbled earth on the sieve over a pale surface
the mineral grit drops through the mesh
the crawling animals stay held above
the tweezers serve to move the animals under the glass without harming them
the wet method means thinning the sample in water and letting the particles settle
the roots and the eggs ride up while the sand sinks
the first method suits looking at whole insects and the second suits gauging how much sand there is
text: You will need a clear jar, a fine sieve, a funnel, a soft pair of tweezers and a magnifying glass. There are two ways to pull the living things out of a soil sample, and they answer different questions. The dry way is to crumble the clod onto the sieve and shake it gently over a pale sheet. Grit and mineral bits drop straight through the mesh, while the crawling animals stay held on top, and the tweezers will carry them under the glass one at a time without hurting them. The wet way is to fill the jar with water, stir the clod into it, then let the mix stand until the particles settle out. Roots and eggs ride up to the top, and the sand goes to the bottom. Take the first way when you are after whole insects to look at, and the second when you want to gauge how much of the sample is sand.

units: a group of about twenty volunteers goes out once the sun is down
their aim is to count the amphibians around a pond
two volunteers help the toads across a road
another post means netting the animals so they can be named
the netted animals go straight back into the water
every sighting is written down with the time and the water temperature
the coordinator says that readings piled up over several seasons bring out trends
one night on its own cannot bring out those trends
the coordinator grants that the conditions are hard and sometimes yield nothing
text: There are about twenty of them, boots on and lamps strapped to their heads, heading down to the pond as soon as the light goes. They are volunteers, and the job of the night is to count amphibians. First station, the road, where two of them pick up the toads crossing it and carry them over to the far side. Second station, the water, where someone dips a net, names the species and puts the animal straight back. Third station, the notebook, where every sighting goes down with the time and the water temperature. Add those figures up season after season, the coordinator says, and trends appear that no single night could ever show. She admits the thankless side too, the cold, the mud, the evenings that turn up nothing. Then a call rises from the ditch and the whole group stops to listen.

units: the calm look of the surface hides the activity underneath
at the end of the cold season the mud on the bottom lets go of bubbles
a greenish film spreads along the edges
jelly-like clumps cling to the plants under water
the embryos come out of their eggs at last
dark larvae gather in swarms near the warmed edge
the larvae feed on the algae coating the stones
the hind limbs form while the tail wastes away
the falling level crowds the last larvae into a small patch of water
the changed animals leave the water for the plants
text: Nothing on the surface of the pond gives away what is going on beneath it. As the cold season loosens its hold, the mud on the bottom lets go of its bubbles and a green film creeps along the edges. Jelly-like clumps show up among the stems, stuck to the reeds under water. They pale, they fill with dark commas, and at last the eggs hatch. Black tadpoles swarm in the warm shallows by the bank, grazing the algae that furs the stones. The shape shifts quietly, with no sign of effort. Back legs push out, the tail wastes away, the skin darkens. Once the heat turns heavy the level drops, the mud cracks open and the last tadpoles crowd together into one narrow puddle. Those that have changed slip off into the tall grass. Next season the clear water will keep no record of any of it.

units: hedgerows are taken out faster than new ones go in
taking those hedgerows out makes room for farm machinery
the wind sweeps the opened ground with nothing in its way
the layer of soil that feeds the crop is carried off into the ditches
rainwater runs down the slopes and cuts channels there
the streams take in more silt
the birds that settled in that brush have grown scarce
fewer such hunters means more spraying against crop insects
replanting is money spent with nothing to show at once
text: Hedgerows are coming out faster than anyone puts them back, and the fields are already showing the bill. Yes, every line of brush removed makes a plot easier to work with machinery. But the wind, which used to break against something living, now sweeps the opened ground and carries the fertile layer off into the ditches. Storm water behaves the same way. It runs straight down the slope, cuts channels as it goes, and loads the streams with silt. The birds that nested deep in the branches have grown scarce, and with them the hunters that kept crop insects in check, so more spraying is needed. A saving in labor is paid back in lost soil, in chemicals and in ditches to clear. Replanting costs money and returns nothing for several seasons. That is exactly why it should start now.
